https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg59.text: Image source, Reuters By James Gregory Published 1 hour ago Warehouses belonging to Russia's second-largest online retailer have been hit by a wave of Ukrainian drone strikes. Ozon said its logistics facilities in the southern regions of Krasnodar, Dagestan, Stavropol and Adygea were on fire and several people had been injured following overnight strikes. Ukraine has for weeks struck sites belonging to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, describing the firm as a legitimate target because it supplied components to the military, which Moscow denies. Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday that Ukraine had opened "Pandora's box" by striking economic targets and that Russia would hit back at Kyiv's "most sensitive economic sectors". Russia has targeted Ukraine's civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022, and recent Russian attacks have hit Ukrainian warehouses and cargo terminals. Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians. Ozon said "a fire broke out" at a logistics centre in Makhachkala, in the southern region of Dagestan, following a drone attack at around 05:00 local time (02:00 GMT) on Monday. The company said earlier that a "major fire" was burning at one of its logistics centres in the city of Krasnodar, 700km (435 miles) to the east of the Dagestan site. Russia's defence ministry said three children had been killed in Krasnodar following a Ukrainian drone attack. Russia's children's rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova said they were aged 13, 15 and 16, while six more children had been taken to hospital. Russia's businesses under strain from Ukraine's attacks on Wildberries Published 23 July Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv Published 48 minutes ago Meanwhile, Ozon workers in Adygeysk, in the Adygea region, and Nevinnomyssk, in the Stavropol region, have been evacuated. Videos posted on social media of the Ozon attacks have been verified by the BBC. One shows a drone hitting a warehouse in the Orenburg region, while another shows a large plume of smoke and flames rising from its warehouse in Dagestan. Shares in Ozon fell by as much as 12% on the Moscow Exchange on Monday morning, while shares in its major shareholder, private equity firm AFK Sistema, fell by almost 13%. When asked on Monday whether the Russian government would provide state support to Ozon, the Kremlin said it was "working with business representatives to develop various options for providing support in this difficult situation". The overnight strikes comes a day after Ozon's site in the Samara region was hit. The company said a number of its workers had been injured. Following that strike, Ukraine's defence ministry said on Saturday: "Systematic strikes on dual-use goods storage centres complicate the enemy's logistics and negatively affect the Russian economy as a whole. "After Ukrainian units hit 15 of the largest logistics hubs of Wildberries, it was Ozon's turn." Meanwhile, in Ukraine's Odesa region, overnight strikes targeted food storage facilities and energy infrastructure leading to five people being injured, the region's head Oleg Kiper said on Telegram. Founded in 1998, Ozon is one of Russia's first online retailers. The company is second only to Wildberries in terms of scale and presence, with its pick-up posts and delivery boxes stationed across the country. Both the Ozon and Wildberries logos are often seen together in Russia at shared pick-up points. The targeting of these online retailers has had the effect of bringing the war closer to ordinary Russians. Both companies have been described as "Russia's Amazon" and it is estimated that they are used by 85-90% of Russia's economically active population. In many remote places lacking accessible shops, Russians depend on them for much of their clothes and household appliances. But unlike Amazon, which sells goods directly alongside its marketplace business, Wildberries and Ozon act almost entirely as marketplaces, connecting independent sellers with buyers across Russia, storing and delivering their goods and handling payments. This means many of the losses incurred in the attacks have been borne by those businesses. The Kremlin has denied that online platforms are used for army supplies. Photograph: Bob Child/AP Books Annie Dillard, Pulitzer prize-winning author of nonfiction and nature essays, dies aged 81 Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, published when Dillard was 28, skyrocketed her to become one of the most prominent nonfiction writers of her generation Marina Dunbar Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.51 EDT Last modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Annie Dillard, author of the Pulitzer prize-winning book Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, died aged 81 at her home in South Wellfleet, Massachusetts on Tuesday. Maggie Nelson, Dillard’s literary editor, confirmed her death to the New York Times . Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, a nonfiction narrative Dillard wrote about the natural world surrounding her mountainous Virginia home, was published in 1974 when the young writer was just 28. The book was an instant critical and financial success, skyrocketing Dillard to becoming one of the most prominent nonfiction writers of her generation. Tinker Creek won the 1975 Pulitzer Prize for general nonfiction, and in 1998 it was included in Modern Library’s list of 100 best nonfiction books. Initially overwhelmed by her sudden fame and countless requests for interviews, the introspective Dillard retreated to Washington state and started splitting her time between the city of Bellingham and the islands Waldron and Lummi. Over the years, Dillard went on to publish poetry, essays, journalism, meditations on religion, theory of literature, two novels and a bestselling autobiography. Her eerie essay, 1982’s Total Eclipse, about her experience witnessing a solar eclipse three years earlier, was chosen by Joyce Carol Oates as among the 20th century’s 100 best essays. Dillard published her autobiography An American Childhood in 1987, which covered her years growing up during the 1950s and 1960s in the Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania area. In 1992, she published her debut novel, The Living, a piece of historical fiction exploring the lives of European settlers and a group of Lummi natives in late 19th century Washington. Dillard was well known throughout her career for her tremendous range as a writer. Her acute ability to capture the astonishment that humans feel in the face of wilderness and the plurality of the world left readers astonished , and her choice to live life surrounded by the wonders of nature was reflected directly in her craft. Her work was often compared to Henry David Thoreau , the naturalist about whom she wrote her master’s thesis. Despite the association, Dillard rejected the pigeonhole label of “nature writer”, instead considering herself a theologian pondering the mystery of God and the duality of reality. In the 1989 collection of short essays, titled The Writing Life, she wrote “how we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives”. Dillard spent her days outdoors taking notes and contemplating everything. Dillard was married three times, most recently to historical biographer Robert D Richardson, whom she was married to for 32 years until his death in 2020. She had one daughter, Cody Rose, born in 1984 in Connecticut. Call the Belgian Embassy In brief: About half of Ukraine’s approximately 43 F-16s are awaiting maintenance in Europe. The Wall Street Journal identified Belgian aerospace company Sabena as the place where some 23 Ukrainian planes sit in maintenance limbo, where the reality is nowhere near a promised four-F-16-per-month turnaround. By Steven Moore Oct. 7, 2026, 3:40 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied (LtoR) A France air force Mirage 2000 D, a France air force Rafale Fighter jet, a Greece air force F 16, a France air force Rafale B fighter jet, a France air force Rafale and a Greece air force F16 fighter jet fly over the southwestern coasts of France on September 26, 2025, as part of the Volfa 2025 national inter-allied and inter-service drills. (Photo by ALAIN JOCARD / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip In Kyiv, we have learned to tell the difference between the softer sound of Russian jet-powered Geran drones and the throaty F-16s that are taking them out. Unfortunately, the sound of the jet Gerans is much more prevalent than that of Ukraine’s defenders. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Almost half of Russia’s jet-powered Gerans are getting through Ukraine’s air defenses. Cumulatively, that is about 4,000 successful strikes this year, attacking bridges, schools and hospitals, with close calls on European embassies and passenger trains full of foreign dignitaries. Russia is building 3,000 per month and expanding production. Many of these strikes could have been intercepted with a fully functioning F-16 fleet. According to President Zelensky, about half of Ukraine’s approximately 43 F-16s are awaiting maintenance in Europe. The Wall Street Journal identified Belgian aerospace company Sabena as the place where some 23 Ukrainian planes sit in maintenance limbo. Advertisement The F-16 is one of the few weapons platforms available to Ukraine that can take out a Russian jet-powered drone. In fact, the faster drones are easier for an F-16 to intercept than the slow-moving propeller-driven Shaheds. Ukraine’s air defenses boast a 90-95% interception rate on those. Ukraine’s F-16 flight wing is one of the most successful of all time. Ukraine flies one of the oldest F-16 fleets with the least experienced pilots, in one of the most brutal air defense environments of any war. Yet they have taken out nearly 700 Russian cruise missiles and more than 2,500 Shahed-type drones , both conventional and jet-powered. For perspective, Royal Air Force fighter planes downed 1,218 Luftwaffe planes in the Battle of Britain. Other Topics of Interest Sweden Sends Patriot to Poland to Guard Ukraine Aid Hub Sweden’s first Patriot mission under NATO command will protect the Rzeszów logistics hub starting in December. But any airplane requires support. “Phase maintenance” is required for every 300 hours of flight time. Belgian aerospace company Sabena was awarded a $235 million contract by the United States Air Force (USAF) to conduct phase maintenance on Ukrainian F-16s in January of this year. Maintenance for a single plane is taking as long as 40 weeks, according to retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery, cited by the Wall Street Journal. Advertisement For comparison, Romanian TV reported in August that phase maintenance for F-16s of the same generation with similar modifications requires six weeks at Romanian aerospace company Aerostar. USAF technicians in 2012 in Kandahar, operating in 40-degree heat under enemy fire, compressed wartime F-16 phase maintenance to three and a half days. Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken , in an interview reminiscent of Monty Python’s “Dead Parrot” sketch , denied any problems, described the Sabena program as “running perfect” and implied that the Wall Street Journal editorial board and a retired two-star admiral might be Russian propagandists. The Sabena contract was awarded in January, and Mr. Francken claims a turnaround of four F-16s per month. Were the program running perfectly, Sabena would have performed 32 phase maintenance procedures this year, and President Zelensky would not be telling the Financial Times about missing half his planes. Certainly, the Dutch seem to think there is a problem, as the Netherlands just announced they will be pitching in on maintenance duties for Ukraine’s F-16s. Advertisement Other Ukrainian F-16 maintenance efforts through Sabena are taking even longer. Norwegian media reported in April of this year that all six F-16s donated to Ukraine in 2023 had been awaiting maintenance or assembly in Belgium for at least a year. Lockheed-Martin can build a new F-16 in less time. Even if Sabena turns over four planes a month going forward, this only addresses Ukraine’s current needs But Mr. Francken seems more interested in saving face than saving lives. Belgium is on both sides of this problem. Brussels should be commended for finally ceasing to import Russian energy in August and September, but Belgian importers have already sent €1.64 billion ($1.84 billion) to Russia for liquid natural gas (LNG) in 2026, according to RussiaFossilTracker. This is enough money to fund the production of every jet-powered Geran Vladimir Putin has fired into Ukraine in 2026, with enough left over to fund about a third of Russia’s cruise missile attacks. One of the last European importers of Russian energy, Belgium ranks among the top five European importers since Jan. 1, 2023, sending about €8.3 billion ($9.3 billion) to Russia in that time frame. For years, we have listened to Belgian officials explaining that a billion-euro contractual obligation to Russia’s Yamal LNG required their gas utility to continue to fund the Russian war machine. Those of us hearing jet-powered Gerans overhead would like to see the same attention paid to contractual obligations by Sabena. Advertisement Even if Sabena turns over four planes a month going forward, this only addresses Ukraine’s current needs and doesn’t return the roughly 29 planes Ukraine has been awaiting. But there is a solution. Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever was very clear at the Victor Pinchuk Foundation’s Ukrainian Breakfast in Davos 2026, when he explained why Russia’s frozen assets should not be used to aid Ukraine’s war effort. He said, “ We are not at war with Russia. Europe is not at war with Russia .” Since Mr. De Wever is not in urgent need of Belgium’s 50 or so F-16s , he could save a lot of lives by instructing the Belgian Air Force to immediately loan Ukraine 29 Belgian F-16s. One Belgian plane will be returned for each Ukrainian plane that returns from maintenance. Belgian loaners would dramatically increase the interception rate of Russian jet-powered Gerans and free Ukrainians from living under terror. It is easy for people living in Ukraine to feel powerless as Russian drones and missiles destroy homes and infrastructure. Now Kyiv residents can act. Call the Belgian embassy and ask them to send replacement F-16s immediately until Sabena can solve its maintenance backlog. Or maybe it is time for the cardboard revolution to shift from Bankova to the Belgian embassy. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Labour Party Conference 2026 in Liverpool - Day Two Secretary of State for the Home Department Shabana Mahmood gives a speech on the second day of the Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, United Kingdom on September 28, 2026. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty Images Immigration and asylum Shabana Mahmood urged to ‘read the room’ on Labour opposition to immigration policy No 10 declines to rule out watering down plans to extend waiting period for indefinite leave to remain as cabinet split widens Rowena Mason and Matthew Weaver Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.33 EDT First published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 06.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Shabana Mahmood has been urged to “read the room” on Labour opposition to her immigration policy, as No 10 declined to rule out watering down her plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency. Mahmood, the home secretary, is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards. She has previously hinted that her plan to make it harder to claim permanent residence could be watered down by exempting care workers from the new rule. However, there were reports on Tuesday that she was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.” View image in fullscreen Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, on Wednesday repeatedly refused to back the plan to make foreign workers wait 15 years to claim permanent residency. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty Images There is already a cabinet split over the policy, which deepened on Wednesday when Miatta Fahnbulleh , the energy secretary, repeatedly refused to back the specific plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to claim permanent residency in the UK. This week it was reported that Fahnbulleh appeared to criticise the plans on her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed. She was quoted as saying: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.” This year the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, publicly criticised the plans , and dozens of Labour MPs oppose the changes. One of the leading opponents, Mike Tapp, a former immigration minister who clashed with Mahmood over the policy, said the home secretary should “read the room” in relation to the strength of feeling about the changes. “It’s important we do the right thing. If people have come to the country and genuinely worked in the sector, they shouldn’t be punished and should have the right to apply for settlement after five years as they expected,” he said. View image in fullscreen MPs believe they have a chance of convincing Burnham to exempt care workers from Mahmood’s proposals. Photograph: 10’000 Hours/Getty Images MPs campaigning for changes to Mahmood’s policies believe they have a chance of convincing Andy Burnham to exempt care workers, given reforming adult social care is an issue close to his heart. However, the Home Office has said that would lead to an exodus of foreign workers from the sector when they are no longer bound by the terms of their visa. No 10 stressed on Wednesday that Mahmood was “carefully considering” more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising the reforms. Asked whether tweaks to the home secretary’s revamp – including no longer applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Burnham’s press secretary said: “We set out proposals for consultation. We’ve consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like for people already in the UK who have not received settled status. “The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion In her interview with Sky News on Wednesday, Fahbulleh repeatedly avoided the question on whether she would back an increase in the waiting period for permanent residency to 15 years. She said: “We have got to reform our immigration system, and my view is that we need a system that is based on the principle of compassion, contribution. And so there is a package of reforms. The home secretary has been consulting on this. She’s looking at the range of responses, and she will come out with the measures that we take forward. “No one can look at our immigration system – and I say this as someone that came to this country as a refugee – and not believe that it’s broken and not believe that we need to fundamentally reform it. “But our principles has to be a system where we’ve got control, but ultimately a system that when people do come to this country, they are able to integrate, they are able to contribute, and that we both respect but also value that contribution.” She said she supported “reforms that say that people have to contribute and make a contribution to this country in order to get citizenship”, adding: “I 100% back Shabana Mahmood and everything she is trying to do.” But she avoided multiple questions on the prospect of a 15-year wait. When it was put to her that she did not back that specific proposal, Fahnbulleh said: “Don’t … put words in my mouth.” A government source said that “the minister clearly supported the policy and process” in her interviews, “but while subject to review of the consultation, the final policy is not set – so ministers cannot offer opinions on specific parts of it”. A Home Office spokesperson said: “This government has announced reforms that mean settlement must be earned and not automatic.
